Dieses Buch lehrt eine Programmiersprach: This book teaches a programming language without ever showing a program that exists only to demonstrate a language rule. Every chapter builds something you enjoy watching: a flight through the stars, a firework, a fractal, a swarm, an instrument, a landscape to fly over. You learn the language along the way — exactly where it is needed, and with the reason why you use it this way and not another at that point.
Das „Warum“ ist der eigentliche Gegensta: The “why” is the real subject of the book. Typing in a program and watching it run is nice, but afterwards you often only know that it works. If you know why the spark is a STRUCT and not five arrays, why the loop counts backwards and why gravity is calculated in pixels per second, you can write the next program yourself. That is why every chapter explains its decisions, names the obvious alternative and says why it would be worse here.
Für alle, die die Grundlagen schon haben: For everyone who already has the basics: variables, loops, decisions, a window with SCREEN. That is the material of the first ten chapters of the book “Der Einstieg” (German), and it is also what you bring along from almost any other programming language. You need little mathematics — wherever a sine or a square root turns up, the chapter explains what it does and shows it in a picture.
ein Bild des Ergebnisses und zwei Sätze: a picture of the result and two sentences about it.
was das Programm tun muss, in Worten, be: what the program has to do, in words, before a single line of code is written.
der Code in kleinen Stücken, nach jedem: the code in small pieces, with an intermediate stage after each step that already runs.
die Entscheidungen, die der Code trifft,: the decisions the code makes, each with the alternative and the reason.
echte Fehler mit den echten Meldungen vo: real mistakes with the real messages from dhrt, word for word, and how to find your way out of them.
in drei Stufen: Drehen (eine Zahl ändern: at three levels: Tweak (change a number and predict what happens), Extend (build something on), Invent (something of your own). Solutions in Appendix A.
die Stellen im Handbuch, die das Thema v: the places in the manual that describe the topic in full.
Am meisten bringt das Buch, wenn man die: You get the most out of the book if you type the programs in rather than copying them. That sounds tedious, and it is a little, but as you type you read every line, and the typos you make along the way are the best teachers: they lead to exactly the messages this book explains.
Und bevor man ein Programm startet, lohn: And before you start a program, a prediction pays off: what is about to happen? If you were right, you have understood. If you were wrong, you have just learned something, and usually more than from a correct guess.
Jedes Programm und jeder Zwischenstand l: Every program and every intermediate stage comes as a file, in the folder buecher/wunder/code of the Drachenhauch repository, and the solutions to the exercises are under code/loesungen. The book prints them from these files, and a test collection runs them with every new version of Drachenhauch: every program compiles, every printed output matches, every error message has the exact wording that dhrt really prints. The pictures, too, come from the programs; none is made by hand.
Hinten im Buch stehen fünf Anhänge: A di: At the back of the book there are five appendices: A the solutions to all exercises, B a cheat sheet of the language, C colours, keys and formulas, D every dhrt message that appears in the book, with its chapter, and E where to go after this book.

On one with 144 the ring turns more than twice as fast, and on an old laptop that only manages 30, half as fast. With DELTA() the numbers in the program are speeds — degrees per second, pixels per second — and the program runs equally fast everywhere. That is why this book always calculates this way.

If you would rather stay in radians, write PI / 6 instead of RAD(30); the result is the same.

Die vier Kapitel dieses Teils malen mit: The four chapters of this part paint with nothing but numbers: a star is a place in space, a colour is an angle, a pattern is a formula, a clock is a rotation. Along the way come the tools that every larger program needs — arrays for many values of the same kind, loops that go through them, functions that give a calculation a name, and constants for everything that is fixed.
Der Sternenflug: vierhundert Sterne komm: Starfield flight: four hundred stars come towards us out of the depths. The nearer a star is, the longer, thicker and brighter its streak.
Sterne fliegen aus der Mitte des Bildes: Stars fly towards us from the centre of the picture, first as tiny dots, then faster and faster outwards, until they vanish at the edge as bright streaks. It is one of the oldest effects in computer graphics, and it needs hardly more than a division.
Ein Stern ist eine Stelle im Raum mit dr: A star is a place in space with three numbers: x (left–right), y (up–down) and z, its distance from us. If we fly towards the stars, only z changes: it gets smaller. On the screen, though, the star moves outwards and gets bigger — and that is exactly what the calculation has to work out. In detail:
bekommt jeder Stern eine zufällige Stell: every star gets a random place in a large box in front of us.

Von der Seite gesehen: Zwei Sterne in de: Seen from the side: two stars at the same height, but at different distances. The ray to the farther one meets the screen closer to the centre.
Stell dir vor, der Bildschirm ist eine G: Imagine the screen is a pane of glass a little way in front of your eye, at distance f. Whatever you see through the pane, you paint onto the glass exactly where the ray to the object passes through it. The picture shows it: two stars are at the same height, 150 above the line of sight, but one is 300 away, the other 680. The ray to the near one meets the glass at 80, the ray to the far one at 35.
Die Rechnung dahinter ist der Strahlensa: The maths behind it is the intercept theorem from school: the small height on the glass is to the distance of the glass as the large height is to the distance of the star. So y' / f = y / z, and rearranged

Mehr ist es nicht. Weil z im Nenner steh: That is all there is to it. Because z is in the denominator, a distant star comes out small and a near one large; and because z gets smaller as we fly, the fraction grows faster and faster — the stars speed up outwards, even though they approach at a steady pace. This is exactly how it looks from a train window: the trees beside the track rush past, the mountains on the horizon barely move.

That sounds pedantic, but it is exactly what you need for tiles, grids and rasters — the tile to the left of 0 has the number -1, not 0. And 8 / 2 is 4.0, not 4: the result of / is always a decimal number, even when the division comes out even.

It is a picture in which every single pixel is recalculated in every frame. That is why this chapter is also about how fast a program is, how you measure that, and what you do when it is too slow.

Die Zahl v ist die Summe von drei Wellen: The number v is the sum of three waves. A wave is a SIN: it swings between -1 and 1, and as x grows it goes up and down like a wave on water. Three waves in different directions overlap to form a pattern of hills and valleys, and it is exactly this pattern that colours the plasma.

Die erste Fassung ist absichtlich die na: The first version is deliberately the obvious one. It is short, easy to understand and shows whether the pattern is pretty at all. Only when it turned out too slow was it measured — and the measurement brought a surprise: the problem was not the calculation with three SINs, but the drawing. Anyone who had “made the formula faster” without measuring would have worked in the wrong place. That is the most important rule about speed: you almost always guess wrong.
Ein kleines Bild statt eines schnelleren: A small picture instead of a faster computer
Die schnellste Arbeit ist die, die man n: The fastest work is the work you don't do. A sixteenth of the pixels means a sixteenth of the work, and that is more than any improvement to the formula could bring. This trade-off — a little less sharpness for a great deal less work — comes up all the time in graphics. There is an even faster way: not calculating the formula in the program at all, but on the graphics card, which calculates millions of pixels at the same time. That is a shader, and Chapter 15 uses one to build the plasma again.

Das Programm läuft, aber statt zu fließe: The program runs, but instead of flowing, the picture flickers wildly. Die Schleife läuft bis 2 · π · 21, also: The loop runs up to 2 · π · 21, that is, over 21 full laps of the wheel around the ring. Why 21, of all numbers? Because that is when the curve first arrives back exactly where it started. Picture the two as gears, the wheel with 84 teeth, the ring with 220. The pen is back at the start when the same tooth of the wheel meshes into the same gap of the ring again. By then, a number of teeth has rolled past that is a multiple of both 84 and 220; the smallest such number is 4620. That makes 4620 / 220 = 21 laps around the ring. You can calculate this as 84 / ggt(220, 84) — with 4 as the greatest common divisor, out comes 21 again.

Computing it is one of the oldest programs in the world: Euclid described it more than two thousand years ago. The greatest common divisor of a and b is the same as that of b and the remainder left over when you divide a by b. And when there is no remainder left, you are done. As a function:

And Drachenhauch protects constants: an assignment to a constant is an error, not a silent change.

Das Spiel des Lebens nach einigen Dutzen: The Game of Life after a few dozen generations: chance has turned into resting blocks, pulsing blinkers and wandering gliders.
Ein Feld aus Zellen, jede lebendig oder: A grid of cells, each one alive or dead. In every generation each cell counts its eight neighbours, and three rules decide whether it lives, dies or is born. That is all there is — no players, no goal. And yet a grid full of chance gives rise to shapes that stand still, pulse or wander across the grid. The mathematician John Conway invented it in 1970, and people have been watching it ever since.
Die drei Regeln, für jede Zelle und ihre: The three rules, for every cell and its eight neighbours:
Eine lebende Zelle mit zwei oder drei le: A living cell with two or three living neighbours lives on.
Eine lebende Zelle mit weniger als zwei: A living cell with fewer than two neighbours dies of loneliness, with more than three of overcrowding.
Eine tote Zelle mit genau drei lebenden: A dead cell with exactly three living neighbours comes alive.
Wichtig ist das Wörtchen „gleichzeitig“:: The little word that matters is “simultaneously”: all cells are judged by the state of the previous generation, and none of them already sees the result of another. How to manage that in a program is the heart of this chapter.

die unten rechts. Eine lebende Zelle ha: the bottom-right one. A living cell has the value 1, a dead one 0. The second array,

The cell itself sits in the middle of that square and gets counted too; that is why the function subtracts it again at the end. That is simpler than checking inside the loop whether you are in the middle right now.

Der wichtigste Satz des Plans war „gleic: The most important word in the plan was “simultaneously”. But a program goes through the cells in turn, one after the other. If it wrote the result straight into the same array, the next cell would already see the new state of its left neighbour and the old state of its right one — a mixture of two generations. With two arrays every cell sees only the previous generation, no matter in which order the program computes. What difference that makes is shown in the section “What can go wrong”.

Das Spiel des Lebens brauchte zwei Felde: The Game of Life needed two arrays because every cell has to see the previous generation. Sand is different: a grain only ever moves into an empty cell. What matters is the order. If the step goes through the world from bottom to top, a grain falls into a row that has already been dealt with, and is not moved again in this step. If it went from top to bottom, it would find the grain again in the next row, the grain would fall once more, and once more — all the way to the floor, in a single step. It is the same consideration as with deleting in Chapter 5: the direction in which you go through an array is part of the calculation.
Für die Seite gilt dasselbe in klein: Wa: The same holds on a small scale for the sideways direction: water that flows to the right afterwards sits in a column the loop has yet to reach, and can flow on in the same step. Water flowing left cannot. So that there is no preferred direction, every second step goes through the rows from right to left.
Bisher hat jedes Programm seine Bewegung: Until now every program measured its movement with DELTA(). But a cell cannot fall 0.3 cells; it falls one or none. That is why the loop adds up the time and takes one step for every sixtieth of a second — on a slow computer two per frame, on a fast one sometimes none. That way the sand trickles at the same speed everywhere. The MIN(…, 0.1) is a brake: if the computer hangs for a second, the program does not catch up on sixty steps at once but on six at most — otherwise the catching up itself would take so long that it would never get back on track.

Within a few seconds they are flying in flocks, turning together, splitting up and coming back together. There is no leader and no plan for the flock. Each bird sees only its neighbours and follows three simple rules. The computer scientist Craig Reynolds wrote them down in 1986 and called his birds “boids”; they have been flying in films and games ever since.

A bird, on the other hand, looks, weighs things up and decides, and for that it needs notes that are nobody else's business — summeX, wegX, neuVx. In a class, the fields and what happens to them are in one place. The main loop needn't know anything about it; it just says v.entscheiden(…) and v.bewegen(…).

If you want to know what a bird does for alignment, you find it in a method of seven lines. And if you want to add a rule — fly to the mouse, avoid rocks, flee from a bird of prey — you write a method and call it in entscheiden. All three exercises at the end of the chapter do exactly that.

But then the program no longer calculates what the plan says: whether a bird already sees another one moved depends on who comes first in the array. With hard rules like those of the Game of Life this becomes a visible error, with soft ones an invisible one — and invisible errors are the more expensive kind.

After ten seconds they are flying on average at only a tenth of the speed they set off with; the flock is almost hovering on the spot. The culprit is alignment: if two neighbours fly in different directions, the average of their velocities is shorter than either one. Every bird adjusts to an average that is a little too slow, frame by frame. Real birds hold their speed by themselves; ours need a method for it.

In this part, things hang from one another, bump into each other, bounce and come gently to rest — and the eye notices at once when it feels wrong.
Zwei Werkzeuge kommen dazu. Das erste is: Two tools join in. The first is mathematics you can write the way you think it: points and directions as one value instead of two numbers. The second is the question of when to calculate such things yourself and when to take ready-made physics. Chapter 9 calculates for itself, Chapter 10 takes the ready-made kind — and explains why that is usually the better choice.

In this chapter we calculate with points and directions, and for that Drachenhauch has the type VEC2 from the vec2 module — a value made of two numbers that you can calculate with as if it were one:

The method is named after the physicist Loup Verlet, who used it for molecules in 1967; in games it has been a common way of doing ropes and cloth for a good twenty years.

Der naheliegende Weg wäre ein anderer: J: The obvious way would be a different one: every link is a spring that pulls when it is too long. Every point has a velocity, which the spring forces and gravity change, as with the sparks in Chapter 5. The program code/kap09/3_federn.dh does exactly that, for the same rope:

And stiff springs explode: in one step a stiff spring pulls so hard that the point overshoots the right distance; in the next step it pulls back even harder, and the point overshoots even further. The stiffer the spring, the smaller the time step would have to be — and a rope that does not stretch would need infinitely stiff springs.

Fertige Physik oder selbst rechnen?: Ready-made physics or calculate it yourself?
Kapitel 9 hat seine Physik selbst gerech: Chapter 9 calculated its physics itself, and that worked because points are simple: they have no size, do not rotate and never bump into anything. A block, on the other hand, has corners. When does a corner touch an edge? How hard does a stack press on the bottom brick? How far does a block slide before friction holds it, and which way does it turn when a ball hits it on the corner? There are good answers to all this, but they fill books. physics2d is the Rapier library, which people have been working on for years.
Darum die Regel: Für feste Körper, die f: Hence the rule: for solid bodies that fall, collide and roll, you almost always take the ready-made physics. You calculate it yourself when the things are not solid bodies — ropes and cloth as in Chapter 9, sand as in Chapter 7, a flock — or when a game is deliberately meant to feel different from reality.

ist nur der Griff, über den man mit ihr: is only the handle through which you talk to it. A body is a number in this world. This is a pattern Drachenhauch uses often — for images, sounds, databases — and it has a price: the number alone does not tell you whether the body still exists. Since this chapter was written, a command given a body that no longer exists stops with a message, and PHYS2D_BODY_EXISTS asks beforehand.
Wie im Sandkasten rechnet die Welt in Sc: As in the sandbox, the world calculates in steps of exactly 1/60 of a second, not in DELTA(). Here there is a second reason: physics with collisions is sensitive. The program code/kap10/3_gleich.dh sends a ball flying four times into the same stack of six blocks, twice in fixed steps and twice in steps that vary like DELTA() — sometimes a little shorter, sometimes a little longer, adding up to exactly two seconds. Then it asks where the top block is lying:
In festen Schritten lag er bei jedem Lau: In fixed steps it lay at x = 487.7 on every run, identical to the tenth. In varying steps it lay at 480.5 and 493.5, on the next start at 462.6 and 460.4, on the one after that at 443.6 and 493.8. A tiny deviation at the first collision grows with every further one. For a game this means: with fixed steps a tower falls the same way for every player, and a bug that someone reports can be reproduced. On top of that, PHYS2D_STEP takes at most 0.05 seconds at a time; if you pass in DELTA() during a stutter, you lose the rest.

Ein Baum ist rekursiv gebaut: Ein Ast mi: A tree is built recursively: a branch with its twigs looks like a small tree. A recursive SUB writes exactly that down — “draw a branch, then two smaller trees at its tip”. With a loop, the program would have to keep track itself of which branch tips are still open, and that is exactly what the turtle does with its stack. Recursion keeps this stack invisibly: every call remembers its x, y and winkel until its two children are finished. Wherever the thing itself is made of smaller versions of itself — trees, folders with subfolders, nested brackets — recursion is the natural form.
Jede rekursive Funktion braucht einen Fa: Every recursive function needs a case in which it no longer calls itself, and every call has to come closer to that case. In ast that is the depth, which gets one smaller with every call until it is 0; the same goes for ausrollen. If either is missing — the check or the getting smaller — the function calls itself without end. What happens then is shown in “What can go wrong”.
Der Bauplan ist Text, und das hat Vortei: The blueprint is text, and that has advantages: you can print it out to see what the turtle is about to do; you can save it, compare it, change it by hand. And a new plant needs no new program, only new rules — the garden has three plants and a single drawing function. The rules are in a MAP because the point is “this text belongs to this character”: looking things up is exactly what a MAP is for.

Drachenhauch counts how deeply the calls are nested inside each other and stops at 1000 — far more than any sensible tree needs, and far less than would get the computer into trouble. The message comes after a fraction of a second.

Teil IV · Bilder, Licht und Farbe: Part IV · Pictures, Light and Colour
Bisher haben die Programme Dinge gezeich: So far the programs have drawn things: points, lines, boxes, now and then a picture. In this part the program calculates the picture itself, pixel by pixel — a landscape made of chance, a fractal, a glow. For that it has to be fast, and for the first time it matters how Drachenhauch actually runs a program.
Das erste Kapitel zeigt, was der Rechner: The first chapter shows what the computer can do if you let it: hundreds of thousands of pixels, each with up to thousands of calculation steps, in fractions of a second. The others show how noise makes clouds, how the graphics card does the calculating itself and why a colour is a number.
Das Seepferdchental, 320-fach vergrößert: Seahorse Valley, magnified 320 times: spirals winding within spirals, and inside them more small black islands. All from a single formula.
Die Mandelbrotmenge ist das bekannteste: The Mandelbrot set is the best-known picture in mathematics. Its formula is so short that it fits on one line, and its edge so intricate that you can zoom in as deep as you like and always find something new — spirals, trunks, stars and, again and again, small copies of the whole set. We build a program that draws it and zooms in with the mouse, and along the way we measure for the first time exactly how fast Drachenhauch calculates, and why.
rechnet das Programm immer wieder z = z: the program calculates z = z · z + c over and over, starting with z = 0.

The difference is machine code. Normally Drachenhauch runs a program in its own little machine, the VM: it reads instruction after instruction and does what each one says. When dhrt notices that a loop or a function runs often, it compiles it into instructions for the processor itself — machine code — and from then on the processor calculates without the detour. This is always switched on; DHRT_JIT=aus is only there for comparison.

Anything beyond that, strings, objects, vectors, it hands over to the VM. 3_messen.dh contains the same calculation a second time, with a VEC2 z as in Chapter 9 instead of two numbers x and y:
Sie ist hübscher zu lesen und liefert ge: It is nicer to read and gives exactly the same eleven million steps — but it takes 3.5 seconds, with machine code or without, more than a hundred times as long as the calculation with numbers. The VEC2 calculation runs in the VM. When this chapter was written, it was even worse: with machine code it took 7.7 seconds, twice as long as without. The machine code compiled the loop but could not carry out the VEC2 calculation inside it by itself, so it handed over to the VM at every step and climbed back in afterwards — the back and forth cost more than it saved. Since then dhrt notices after a few rounds that a loop bails out every time, and leaves it in the VM. With DHRT_JIT_BILANZ=1 it also tells you which one: “loop at position 6 in mitvec2 stays in the VM”. The rule stands: only numbers belong in the innermost loop of a program that calculates millions of steps.

Reality hangs together — next to a high point lies one almost as high. Noise has exactly this property and is still unpredictable. It was invented in 1983 by Ken Perlin for film effects; since then it has been behind almost every landscape, every cloud and every fire that a computer shows.

FBM imitates exactly that — each layer half as large and half as strong as the one before. The large layers decide where there is land; the small ones make the edges rough. Six layers are enough here: the seventh would be smaller than a pixel.

Ein Prozessor hat einige wenige Kerne, j: A processor has a few cores, each very fast and very clever: it can jump, wait, make decisions and remember everything. A graphics card has thousands of arithmetic units, each one slower and simpler, but all working at the same time. They get the same program and each one a different pixel. For the plasma that is ideal: every pixel is calculated with the same formula, and none needs the result of another.
Diese Arbeitsteilung hat einen Preis. Ei: This division of labour has a price. A shader can only write its own pixel, not the one next to it. It can read what is in the picture, but not what it is calculating itself right now. And it forgets everything as soon as the frame is finished. That is why the Game of Life from Chapter 6 or the sand from Chapter 7 cannot simply be written as a shader: there every cell depends on the previous state of its neighbours, and the sand falls grain by grain in a particular order. The memory of the light trails — the sheet that slowly fades — therefore lives in the program, in a render target. The shader does only what it does best: apply the same calculation to every frame.
Ein uniform ist für alle Bildpunkte glei: A uniform is the same for all pixels and changes at most once per frame. That is exactly what the time, the size of the window and the strength of the glow are. Everything that changes from pixel to pixel the shader works out itself from fragTexCoord. This separation — a few values from the program, the hard graft on the graphics card — is the reason why shaders are so fast.

The program runs anyway, but the plasma stands still, because its uniform zeit never gets a value. When this chapter was written there was no message for this yet — all you saw was a picture that did not move. Since then SHADER_SET warns once per name. It is similar with a mistyped file name: SHADER_LOAD("plasm.fs") is a run-time error that names the file and the folder where it looked.

The shader is not compiled by Drachenhauch but by the graphics card's driver; the message comes from the driver, in English, and looks a little different on every graphics card. This one comes from an NVIDIA card. 0(8) means line 8: the compiler only notices the missing semicolon at the next word, finalColor. SHADER_LOAD then returns −1 instead of a shader, and POSTFX(−1) merely switches off — the program carries on with a picture without a shader. That is why 1_plasma.dh checks whether loading worked.

The reason is rounding: a colour is stored as a whole number from 0 to 255. 31 · 251/255 is 30.5 and becomes 31 again. From then on the trail gets no darker, however often you multiply — measured, it stayed at 31 out of 255, 12 per cent brightness. Subtracting 1 pushes it past this threshold: what is almost black becomes completely black.

Warum eine Farbe eine Zahl ist: Why a colour is a number
Jeder Bildpunkt eines Bildschirms besteh: Every pixel on a screen consists of three tiny lights: red, green and blue. Each can have 256 brightnesses, from 0 to 255, and 256 possibilities are exactly eight binary digits. Three lights need 24 digits, and they fit comfortably into one number. 256 · 256 · 256 makes 16.7 million colours — more than an eye can tell apart. Hexadecimal is the handiest way to write colours, because each of the three colours has exactly two digits. Drachenhauch uses the eight digits in front for the opacity: RGBA(255, 160, 32, 128) is a half-transparent orange.
Warum BAND schwächer bindet als +: Why BAND binds more weakly than +
Malnehmen geht vor Plus — das kennt jede: Times comes before plus — everybody knows that from school. For BAND, BOR, SHL and SHR there is no school rule; Drachenhauch does it like C, Java and Python: they bind more weakly than + and −. If you write a BAND b + c, you get a BAND (b + c). There is a reason for this: bit operations mostly work on finished numbers — a colour, a mask —, and you should be able to work those out before you take them apart. But it is a trap, and that is why Drachenhauch warns you when a + or − stands next to a BAND without brackets. The simplest rule: if you mix bit operations with arithmetic, use brackets.
Um 1990 hatte ein Rechner für das Bild 6: Around 1990 a computer had 64,000 bytes for the picture: 320 by 200 pixels, one byte per pixel. That was not enough for 24 digits per pixel; but a byte holds a number from 0 to 255. When displaying, the graphics card looked up each number in a table of 256 colours. If a program changed a colour in this table, every pixel with that number changed — all at once, and without the program touching a single pixel. That is how the glittering waterfalls, flickering fires and pulsing lights of the games of that time were made.
Heute ist es umgekehrt. Beim Abendsee br: Today it is the other way round. For the evening lake, malen needs about 6.5 milliseconds for all 25,000 pixels, but drawing from the numbers takes 11 milliseconds per frame: the 25,000 PLOTs are the expensive part, not the arithmetic. What the palette brings today is the separation: the picture says where the lake is, the palette says what it looks like. Night, winter or a glittering lake change 18 numbers and know nothing about rocks and mountains. If you need it faster, you send the numbers as an image to a shader as in Chapter 15 and let the graphics card do the looking up — that is exactly how emulators for old games do it.

Warum ein Bild, das bleibt, ein eigenes: Why a picture that stays needs a target of its own
Man könnte meinen, das Fenster sei selbs: You might think the window itself is a sheet: whatever you draw stays there until you paint over it. That really was how it worked on the home computers of the eighties, and some simple drawing programs still behave that way today. Not in Drachenhauch, and the reason is flicker.
Würde ein Programm direkt in das Bild ma: If a program painted directly into the picture you are looking at, you would see it being painted: half-erased shapes, parts of the old picture over the new one. That is why almost every graphics system today draws into a picture you cannot see yet and only shows it once it is finished; FLIP is called that because it flips the two over. Afterwards the invisible picture is no longer the one from a moment ago — often it is the one from two frames back, or its content is not defined at all. Drachenhauch goes one step further: at first it only remembers what is to be drawn, and at FLIP it draws everything onto a freshly cleared surface. If you draw one circle per frame without CLS, you therefore only ever see one.
Ein Bild, das wachsen soll, braucht also: So a picture that is meant to grow needs memory of its own that nobody clears: the render target with TRUE. It is a picture on the graphics card like the window, only you cannot see it until RENDERTARGET_DRAW stamps it onto the window. That costs one rectangle per frame — nothing at all for the graphics card.
Drehen in x und y geht auch: x′ = x · co: Rotating in x and y works too: x′ = x · cos w − y · sin w, y′ = x · sin w + y · cos w. It is the same calculation, only the angle is hidden inside it, and you cannot tell by looking at it that it is a rotation. In polar coordinates it says w + dreh, and you can read that. Then there is mirroring: in x and y, mirroring at a slanted axis is a formula of its own; in polar coordinates it is a minus in front of the angle. The rule behind this holds far beyond this chapter: you calculate in the description in which the task is simple, and only convert back at the very end.
Ein Tastendruck dauert für einen Mensche: To a human a key press is short, but to a program running at 60 frames per second it lasts five to ten frames. With KEY_DOWN, M would toggle mirroring in every one of those frames — on, off, on, off — and in the end it would be down to chance whether it is on. KEY_HIT holds only in the frame in which the key goes down, and so it toggles exactly once. The same question comes up with the mouse: MOUSE_DOWN for painting as long as the button is down, MOUSE_HIT for something that should happen once when you click.

Das Ohr hört Verhältnisse, nicht Abständ: The ear hears ratios, not differences. Going from 110 to 220 Hz sounds just as much like “one octave higher” as going from 880 to 1760 Hz, although the difference is 110 Hz in one case and 880 Hz in the other. To the ear, a step means multiplying by a factor, and multiplying only turns into adding once you take the logarithm. That is why the keys of a piano are all the same width, although the frequencies grow faster and faster towards the right, and that is why the program says 2 to the power of x. The twelve equal steps per octave are called equal temperament; they are a compromise in which no key sounds better than any other — the exercise with the two voices hears the difference.
Mit der Lautstärke ist es genauso. Ein T: It is just the same with volume. A tone with the factor 0.5 does not sound half as loud, only a little quieter; it only sounds half as loud at about a third. The ear compares ratios — from 1 to 0.1 is the same step as from 0.1 to 0.01. Decibels count these steps: −20 dB is a tenth, −40 dB a hundredth. If the program spread the factor evenly over the height, almost the whole upper half of the window would be loud, and everything quiet would be squeezed into a narrow strip along the top edge. With decibels, every centimetre upwards sounds equally much quieter.
Das Tremolo könnte das Programm auch sel: The program could also calculate the tremolo itself. But the program only comes round 60 times per second, and when a frame takes longer because Windows happens to be doing something else, the tremble falters audibly. A modulator runs on the audio thread, which calculates every single sample, 48,000 times per second. It never falters, and the program has to do nothing for it. However, a modulator only drives what hangs on a bus: volume, balance, filter, reverb, distortion. The pitch of a channel is not one of them — so a vibrato, a trembling of the pitch, has to be calculated by the program itself. The second exercise does that and measures whether you can hear it.

Ein Bild dauert eine sechzigstel Sekunde: A frame lasts a sixtieth of a second. In such a short time music fluctuates wildly: a tone wavers with beating, a drum is almost over after 50 ms, and the FFT sees a different slice every time. If the picture showed every measurement as it is, the bars would twitch so fast that the eye sees only flicker. Smoothing means: each new value counts only in part, the old one lingers on. The eye then sees movement instead of noise. AUDIO_FFT already smooths a little by itself — a band does not drop at once but to 80 % in every sixtieth of a second — and on top of that the program smooths what it calculates itself.
Nicht jeder Bildschirm zeigt 60 Bilder j: Not every screen shows 60 frames per second. Many show 120 or 144, and a slow computer may manage only 30. If you take a fixed share of the distance per frame, you smooth faster on a fast screen and more slowly on a slow one — the program behaves differently everywhere. That is why glaetten and the peaks calculate with DELTA(). While trying things out for this chapter, it turned out that AUDIO_FFT itself had this bug: it let the bands fall per call. If you asked it every 4 ms, a band was down to 0.03 by 50 ms after the tone; if you asked it every 16 ms, it was at 0.33. Now it calculates with the time since the last call.
Warum die tiefen Balken in Gruppen stehe: Why the low bars stand in groups
Links sind immer mehrere Balken gleich h: On the left, several bars are always the same height, at the far left even six. The FFT works with 1024 samples, and from those it can only tell frequencies apart in steps of 47 Hz (48,000 divided by 1024). At 50 Hz one step is almost an octave wide, at 5000 Hz only a hundredth of that. The lowest six bands all fall into the same step and show the same value. More samples would give a finer resolution but look further back: 4096 samples are already almost a tenth of a second, and a drum would be smeared in the picture. 1024 is a compromise between precise and fast.
Drei Werte aus einer Funktion zu holen,: You could also get three values out of a function by using three functions — but then the program would go over the array three times, and nothing would say that the three belong together. Global variables would work too, but then any part of the program can change them. A tuple holds together what comes into being together: bass, mids and highs from the same moment. Classes would be the other option; a tuple is lighter when the values are unpacked again right away.

Teil VI · Die Sprache für Fortgeschritte: Part VI · The Language for the Advanced
Die Programme werden größer, und damit w: The programs are getting bigger, and with that it becomes important how you organise them. This part shows the means by which you divide a large program into pieces that each stay understandable on their own: classes that inherit from each other, functions as values, routines that can wait, data reshaped in a single line, errors that you catch. Along the way, each chapter asks when a tool helps and when it only makes things harder to read.
Ein Feuer mit Rauch, Schnee und — der Ma: A fire with smoke, snow and — following the mouse — a shower of sparks. Four effects from one construction kit.
Ein Baukasten für Effekte. Ein Feuer bre: A construction kit for effects. A fire burns, smoke rises above it and drifts in the wind, snow falls across the whole picture, and wherever the mouse is, magic sprays out — the space bar switches it between a shower of sparks, a whirl and bubbles. All of them are made of particles, small circles that appear, move, change their colour and vanish. The only thing that sets them apart is how they begin, how they move and what colour they are. This chapter shows two ways of writing such differences: as subclasses that inherit and override, and as recipes made of lambdas. And it asks when which one is better.

Warum man meistens das Lambda will: Why you usually want the lambda
Drei Anfänge, drei Arten zu ziehen und d: Three beginnings, three ways of pulling and three colourings make 27 effects. As classes that would be 27 subclasses, and every new colouring would need nine new ones. As recipes it is three lines per part, which you plug together freely — the second Extend exercise does exactly that. Inheritance binds together what should stay together; lambdas keep apart what you want to mix. That is why many programs today have a small class that provides the framework, and lambdas that supply the behaviour. The particle machine has both: Effekt is the framework, Rezept the plugboard.

With ABSTRACT, compiling already stops, because the fire does not fill in the announced method. An error while compiling is the cheapest there is.

Eine kleine Szene auf einer Lichtung: De: A little scene in a clearing: the dragon has sneezed, and the stars have come out in the sky.
Eine kleine Geschichte, die von selbst a: A little story that plays out by itself. A dragon comes into a clearing and asks whether anyone is there. After a pause a hedgehog arrives and complains that the dragon is waking the forest. The dragon apologises — he is only practising his fire — then sneezes sparks three times, and at the end the stars come out. Every game has scenes like this: a cutscene, a tutorial, a character telling you something. The hard part is not the drawing but the waiting: the program has to draw a frame 60 times per second and still know where in the story it is. This chapter shows two ways of writing that down — and why the second one reads like a script.

So schreibt man es, wenn man nur Schleif: This is how you write it when all you have is loops and variables. The main loop runs through once per frame and has to work out afresh every time where it is. That is what the number in zustand is for: 0 is the silence at the start, 1 the walking dragon, 2 the speaking one, and so on. SELECT CASE jumps to the state, and each state checks whether it is over; if so, it prepares the next one and switches over. This works, and for a section like “the dragon walks until he stands still” it is even easy to follow. But after only six states the story is hard to read: what happens one after another sits in boxes side by side, and anyone who wants to insert a line has to shift numbers around. And the three sneezes, a loop in your head, would be three states here, or a counter you have to keep yourself.

Warum die Koroutine lesbarer ist: Why the coroutine is easier to read
Beide Fassungen tun dasselbe. Der Unters: Both versions do the same thing. The difference is where the sequence is written down. In the state machine it lives in the transitions: to find out what comes after state 3, you look for the line naechster(4) and then for CASE 4. In the coroutine it lives in the order of the lines — the next line comes next, as in any program that does not wait. The program itself remembers where it is, namely at the YIELD; in the state machine you have to remember it yourself with zustand, uhr and dauer. That is why sequences that stretch over many frames — a scene, a tutorial, an enemy's attack — are often written as coroutines.
Warum der Zustandsautomat trotzdem seine: Why the state machine still has its place
Ein Automat ist besser, wenn es keine fe: A state machine is better when there is no fixed order: a player character can stand, run, jump and fall, and from almost any state it can go to almost any other, depending on what the player presses. That is not a script but a web, and for that, numbered states with transitions are exactly right; the module animfsm helps with this. Rule of thumb: if there is an “after that”, use a coroutine; if there is a “depending on”, use a state machine.
Warum die Koroutine nicht selbst wartet: Why the coroutine does not do its own waiting
Die Koroutine könnte auch selbst die Sek: The coroutine could count the seconds itself as well: YIELD 0 in a loop and warte = warte − DELTA(). But then every wait would have to contain that loop. This way the script only says how long, and the driver takes care of it — in one place. That is also where skipping can be built in without touching the script.
Kapitel 21, was schiefgehen kann: ein He: Chapter 21, what can go wrong: a helper with YIELD, called in the scene
Es liegt nahe, das Warten in einen Helfe: It is tempting to put the waiting into a helper: warten(2). But a helper with YIELD is itself a coroutine, and called as a statement it only returns its handle, which nobody keeps. So no time passes between “wartet” and “spricht”. YIELD only ever stops the function it is in, never the one that called it. When this chapter was written there was no message for this; now Drachenhauch warns. If you really want to pass on a helper's steps, keep the handle and resume it yourself — the manual shows how. Usually it is simpler to do what the scene does: YIELD with the waiting time.
Steht in szene kein einziges YIELD mehr: If szene no longer contains a single YIELD — say because you deleted them all while reworking it — it is not a coroutine but an ordinary function: szene() runs straight through at once and returns its number. Previously that number landed silently in the COROUTINE variable, and the error only came at the next CORO_RESUME. Now compiling already warns, and the assignment stops with: “expected COROUTINE, got FLOAT -- only a call of a FUNCTION or SUB that contains YIELD gives a coroutine”.
Kapitel 21, was schiefgehen kann: das Dr: Chapter 21, what can go wrong: the script as a SUB, without RETURN.
Das letzte CORO_RESUME, das die Koroutin: The last CORO_RESUME, the one that ends the coroutine, returns its RETURN value. A SUB has none, so NIL comes back — and NIL does not fit into a FLOAT variable. That is why szene is a FUNCTION … AS FLOAT with RETURN 0 at the end: the last value is a waiting time like any other.

Ein ganzes Jahr Wetter auf einem Bild. J: A whole year of weather in one picture. Each day is a ray that begins at the lowest temperature and ends at the highest; January is at the top, and from there the year runs round clockwise. The colour tells you how warm it was, and the blue dots on the outside are rainy days — the bigger, the more rain. On the left is what sums up the year: the warmest and the coldest day, how much rain fell and how long the sun shone. The data come from a file with 365 rows. How to turn a file like that into columns, maximums and averages with a few lines of code is what this chapter is about — with comprehensions, a short way of writing “take everything from this list that …, and turn it into …”.

Echte Wetterdaten gibt es bei jedem Wett: Real weather data is available from every weather service, but each one writes it down a little differently. So we invent a year of our own that looks real enough. The season is a cosine curve: on average 0 degrees in mid-January and 20 degrees in mid-July. On top of that comes a deviation that is not rolled afresh every day but drifts slowly — each day it keeps 85 per cent of yesterday’s value and gets a little randomness added. That way warm and cold weeks appear, as in real weather, instead of the temperature jumping back and forth from day to day. Rain tends to fall on cool days, and when it does, it is mostly a little and rarely a lot; the sun shines for as long as the day is long, but less when it rains.

Es gibt zwei Sorten Fehler. Die einen ko: There are two kinds of error. Some come from outside: a broken file, a network that does not answer, an input that is not a number. The program cannot prevent them, only be ready for them — that is what TRY is for. The others the program makes itself: an index that does not exist, a mistyped name, a division by zero. You do not catch those, you avoid them. The empty bilder, the missing titel.txt: the slideshow asks about both beforehand, with LEN and FILEEXISTS. An error in your own program that gets caught is only hidden.
Warum das TRY so eng ist: Why the TRY is so narrow
Um die Schleife steht kein großes TRY, s: There is no big TRY around the loop, but a small one around each file, with only two lines in it. The more a TRY contains, the more errors it catches, including ones that do not come from outside at all — and then it reports them as “file broken”. What that looks like is shown under “What can go wrong”. A narrow TRY says exactly what you are expecting.
Das CATCH für die Titel entscheidet nach: The CATCH for the titles decides by ERROR_CODE$, not by the text of the message. Texts change: while this chapter was being written, even the message from LOADIMAGE changed (see below). Anyone who had checked its wording would now be broken. A code like TITEL is an agreement between two places in your own program, and the message may change without anything breaking. Built-in errors have the code "" — so every one of them falls into the “rethrow” branch of the title CATCH.

A TRY with neither CATCH nor FINALLY swallows every error, and that is almost never what you meant. When this chapter was written, Drachenhauch said nothing about it; now it warns. If you really want to pass over an error, write an empty CATCH — then every reader can see that it is deliberate.

Bis hierher war alles flach. In diesem l: Until now everything was flat. In this last part the world gains depth: solid bodies in space, a camera you carry around, light, shadow and haze, a landscape to fly into. The programs do not get much longer, because the hard part — which point of the world lands where on the screen — is worked out by the graphics card. At the end, everything the book has shown comes together in a demo with music that you can pass on to others.
Eine Windmühle auf einer Wiese: Die Flüg: A windmill in a meadow: the sails turn and cast shadows, and in the distance trees and houses blur into the haze.
Die dritte Dimension. Eine Windmühle ste: The third dimension. A windmill stands in a meadow, its sails turn slowly, and its shadow wanders across the grass. Around it are two houses and a few fir trees, and further back everything blurs into the haze. Hold down the mouse button to turn the camera around the mill; the mouse wheel brings you closer. The program is no longer than the two-dimensional ones of the last chapters. Three things are new: a camera that decides where you look from; light that makes surfaces bright and dark; and matrices that let one part hang on another — the sails on the hub.

Dreitausend Bäume, einmal mit einem MODE: Three thousand trees, once with one MODEL per tree and once with one MODEL_INSTANCED for all of them. On the computer this book was written on, the first way costs 7.1 milliseconds per frame, the second 0.2 — about thirty-five times less. At sixty frames per second a frame has just under 17 milliseconds; with MODEL the trees alone would take almost half of that.
Der Grund ist nicht das Zeichnen selbst,: The reason is not the drawing itself; the graphics card does that equally fast in both cases. What is expensive is the asking: every MODEL call sends the graphics driver a job of its own with everything that goes with it, and the driver checks and sets everything up anew each time. With MODEL_INSTANCED there is a single job: here is the model, here are three thousand matrices, draw them all. That is why many identical things — trees, grass, stars, stones, building blocks — are drawn as instances. The price: instances cannot cast shadows and cannot reflect like MODEL_PBR; for a single windmill you still use MODEL.

A model is there to be drawn, not to be asked questions. So the numbers are kept once in the array, and picture, forest and flight all ask the same source. That way they always fit together.

Zum Schluss alles zusammen. Eine Demo, w: To finish, everything together. A demo of the kind people have been making since the eighties: a small program that wants nothing more than to show, for one minute, what a computer can do. Ours has three scenes. First, sparks rise through a starry sky and a title glows into view. Then the camera flies over an evening landscape with mountains and forest. Finally, the end credits scroll upwards and the music fades away. In between it goes dark for a moment, and over everything lies the glow from Chapter 15.
Fast nichts daran ist neu — Partikel, Mu: Almost nothing in it is new — particles, music from AUDIO_NOTE, a shader, terrain and instances are all familiar. What is new is how you build something this big without losing track: in five files, each of which does one thing and knows as little as possible about the others.

Fertig ist ein Programm erst, wenn ander: A program is only finished when others can start it — without Drachenhauch. dhrt --export compiles the demo together with all the included files and attaches it to a copy of the runtime; out comes a folder demo_dist with a demo.exe. The folder assets is copied along: that is why the shader lives there and not next to demo.dh, because the export cannot find a file by itself if the program only loads it while running. The exported demo runs from any folder — on start-up it changes to the folder it lives in, and so finds its assets. Tried out: started from an unrelated folder, the title glows just as in dhrt.
Der Export nimmt die kleinste Laufzeit,: The export takes the smallest runtime that knows all the commands of the demo. You can zip the folder and send it, put it on a USB stick or on a web page. The demo does not fit into the playground in the browser, though: the playground takes a program from a single text box and shares it via a link, with no further files and no shaders. For a single program like those in the first chapters, it is the fastest way to show it; for a demo, the exported file is.
Warum ein großes Programm in kleine Teil: Why a big program goes into small parts
Die Demo ist zusammen gut 300 Zeilen lan: Altogether the demo is a good 300 lines long. In a single file, every line would be connected to every other: a variable sx, a CONST N, a function boden — any of them could be used anywhere and changed anywhere. Anyone changing something in the landscape would have to know whether the end credits depend on it. Splitting it up cuts these connections. Whatever still flows between the parts is visible in one place: in the clock, as calls like flug.zeichnen(zeit). You can read, change or replace a scene, or take it along into another program, without touching the others.
Der Schnitt geht dort, wo sich etwas una: The cut goes where something can change independently. The music has nothing to do with the pictures, except for its length — so it gets one file, with dauer() as the only connection. The scenes have nothing to do with one another, they only share the same structure. What occurs in almost every scene, the fade, belongs to the clock. A good rule of thumb: if you can give a part a name that says in three words what it does, it is probably cut well.

vorbereiten, zeichnen, beenden — jede Sz: vorbereiten, zeichnen, beenden — every scene looks the same from outside. With -40 the ring turns the other way. Because y grows downwards on the screen, a growing angle runs clockwise and a shrinking one anticlockwise. With 400 it turns ten times as fast, one full turn in 0.9 seconds — and the breathing becomes ten times as fast too, because the radius depends on the same angle (drehung * 3). A program that ties two movements to one quantity changes both when you tweak that quantity.
Die Farbtöne reichen jetzt nur noch von: The hues now only reach from 0 to 165 degrees: red, orange, yellow, green, up to a greenish turquoise. Blue, violet and pink are missing, and between the last circle and the first the colour jumps from turquoise back to red. Only twelve times thirty gives the full 360 degrees of the colour wheel.
i * 30 steht dreimal im Programm: im Win: i * 30 appears three times in the program: in the angle, in the breathing and in the colour. For 24 circles it has to be i * 15 everywhere, because 24 times 15 is 360 again. If you forget the angle, circles 13 to 24 sit in the same places as 1 to 12 — you only see twelve. If you forget the colour, the rainbow goes round twice. If you forget the breathing, the wave runs round the ring twice; that is not a mistake, just a different pattern. So that 24 circles do not overlap, the radius may get smaller, say 16 + SIN(…) * 6.
Eine zweite Schleife nach der ersten, mi: A second loop after the first, with a smaller distance from the centre, smaller circles and an angle that runs twice as fast and the other way (code/loesungen/kap00_zwei_ringe.dh):
Die Farbe ist um 180 Grad verschoben: Je: The colour is shifted by 180 degrees: every inner circle has the opposite colour of the outer circle with the same number. The variables are called wi, xi and yi instead of w, x and y — that would not be necessary, because a DIM in a loop starts afresh every time round, but this way you can see while reading which calculation belongs to which ring.
Mit DELTA() dreht sich der Ring genauso: With DELTA() the ring turns just as fast as before, only more jerkily: it now jumps fifteen times a second by 2.7 degrees each time instead of sixty times by 0.67. The version with the fixed step turns four times as slowly, because it still moves 0.67 degrees per frame, and there are only a quarter as many frames. That is exactly what happens when a computer is too slow to manage sixty frames.
Mit 100 rückt alles zur Mitte: Die Stern: With 100 everything moves towards the centre: the stars stay small dots for a long time and only shoot outwards right at the end, and the picture looks wide and deep. With 900 you only see the middle part of the starfield, greatly magnified; the stars leave the picture quickly, and the flight looks fast and flat. That is the difference between a wide-angle lens and a telephoto lens — the focal length of a camera is exactly the number f from the drawing.
Viertausend Sterne machen aus dem Nebel: Four thousand stars turn the haze in the centre into a bright cloud; whether that is prettier is a matter of taste. The program does not get noticeably slower: on the computer this book was written on, it ran much faster than the screen can show frames, even with twenty thousand stars. A loop over a few thousand numbers is no work at all for a computer.
Das Programm bricht nach einem Augenblic: After a moment the program stops with the message “RGB-Werte muessen 0..255 sein”. The first star that flies past us gets a negative z, so naehe = 1 - z / TIEFE becomes greater than 1 and the brightness greater than 255. So that one line protects three things at once: the division from 0, the picture from mirrored stars and the colour from values above 255. Before you take out a protective line like this, think about who relies on it.

Blau (Farbton 220), das mit der Naehe bl: Blue (hue 220) that gets paler with nearness: far away
strong blue, right at the front almost white.
Die Helligkeit hell, die bisher in alle: The brightness hell, which so far went into all three colour components, becomes the third value of HSV, divided by 255, because HSV expects a number from 0 to 1 there. So distant stars stay dark and blue, near ones bright and almost white — as on a clear night, when the light of distant things looks bluish.
Statt der Konstante TEMPO fliegen die St: Instead of the constant TEMPO, the stars now fly with a variable flug that follows the desired speed (code/loesungen/kap01_warp.dh):
Das Ziel springt, flug folgt ihm in etwa: The target jumps; flug follows it in about half a second.
(flug, nicht tempo: das hiesse wie die C: (flug, not tempo: that would be the same name as CONST TEMPO.)
Die Zeile flug = flug + (ziel - flug) *: The line flug = flug + (ziel - flug) * MIN(1.0, 4 * dt) closes a large part of the gap to the target every second, quickly at first, then more and more slowly; that is the gradual speed-up. The MIN prevents overshooting the target when a frame takes very long (dt large). The variable is called flug and not tempo: because Drachenhauch does not distinguish between upper and lower case, tempo would be the same as the constant TEMPO, and the program would not compile. Chapter 4 comes back to this.

Mit Stift 120 sitzt der Stift außerhalb: With pen 120 the pen sits outside the wheel, as if on an arm. The arcs of the curve become loops that wind around each other on the way inwards; the curve reaches further out and further in than before. With pen 0 the pen sits exactly in the centre of the wheel and does not take part in its rotation: it draws a simple circle with radius 220 - 84 = 136, the path of the wheel's centre.

With pen 110 the ellipse becomes completely flat: the pen moves back and forth along a straight line, right across the ring. A wheel rolling in a ring twice its size turns a rotation into a straight movement — this is known as Cardan's circles and was used in machines long before there were computers. In numbers: innen / rad is then 1, and with stift = 110 the two SIN terms in kurveY cancel each other out exactly.

Mit 0.05 sind zu wenige Zellen da, um ei: With 0.05 there are too few cells to keep each other alive: almost everything dies in the first generations, leaving a few lonely blocks and blinkers. With 0.7 it is too crowded: almost everything dies of overcrowding, and from the remains grows a picture similar to the one at 0.25, only later. Life needs a medium density — somewhere between a fifth and a half is where the most comes about.
Mit Geburt auch bei sechs Nachbarn heißt: With birth also at six neighbours, the variant is called HighLife. Most of it looks as before, but every now and then a pattern turns up that copies itself: the replicator. It leaves behind a trail of copies of itself. A single number in the rules changes what is possible in the world.
Drei Zellen waagrecht nebeneinander: Die: Three cells side by side horizontally: the middle one has two neighbours and survives, the two outer ones have only one each and die. Above and below the middle one there is a dead cell with exactly three living neighbours — they are born. The horizontal row becomes a vertical one, and in the next generation a horizontal one again: the blinker blinks, for ever.
Die Zelle unter der Maus ist die Mausste: The cell under the mouse is the mouse position divided by the cell size as a whole number, plus one, because the array starts at 1 (code/loesungen/kap06_maus.dh):
Die Zelle unter der Maus: ganzzahlig tei: The cell under the mouse: divide as whole numbers, count from 1.
MOUSE_DOWN statt MOUSE_HIT: Solange die: MOUSE_DOWN instead of MOUSE_HIT: as long as the button is held down, you draw, as with a pen. Checking the bounds protects against an index outside the array when the mouse is at the edge of the window.

(x - 1) MOD B rechnet die Spalte auf 0 b: (x - 1) MOD B converts the column to 0 to B - 1, and + 1 brings it back to 1 to B. For x = 0, (x - 1) MOD B in Drachenhauch is B - 1, because MOD rounds down like \ does, even for negative numbers — in many other languages the result would be -1, and you would need an extra + B. A glider that flies out at the bottom right now comes back in at the top left.
Eine Möglichkeit (code/loesungen/kap06_a: One possibility (code/loesungen/kap06_alter.dh): instead of 0 and 1, the array holds the age of the cell. lebt still answers with 0 or 1, so that the rules stay the same; only a birth sets 1, and survival counts up:
In den Feldern steht jetzt das Alter: 0: The arrays now hold the age: 0 dead, 1 just born, 2 means ...
lebt seit zwei Generationen. Fuer die Re: alive for two generations. For the rules, all that counts is: is it alive?

Wer geboren wird, ist eine Generation al: A cell that is born is one generation old.
Hier zahlt sich die Funktion lebt ein zw: Here the function lebt pays off a second time: nachbarn hardly had to change at all, because it never looked at the array itself. Only subtracting the cell itself now asks lebt instead of the array — otherwise it would subtract the cell's age instead of a 1.
Das Wasser wird zäh wie Honig. Unter der: The water becomes as thick as honey. Under the nozzle a hump grows that spreads out only slowly, and on the board the water builds up instead of flowing down. One cell per step is too slow to keep up with the supply; four are fast enough for the lake to look level. Real water has no cells, but the same question — how quickly it gives way — is what tells water from honey there too.
Die Sandhaufen bleiben, wie sie waren: I: The sand piles stay as they were: if the left is occupied, a grain simply slides to the right, and 45 degrees is the only slope that holds on either side. The water, however, now flows only to the left. It runs off the left end of the board, fills the floor to the left of the nozzle, and to the right of it everything stays dry. The difference: sand only moves when it can fall, and falling is the same on both sides. Water moves horizontally as well, and there s alone decides which way.
Alles läuft viermal so schnell, und weil: Everything runs four times as fast, and because the nozzles give one grain and one drop per step, four times as much comes out in the ten seconds: a big pile, a deep lake. The shapes stay the same — 45 degrees, level water — because the rules know nothing about seconds, only about cells. TAKT alone determines how often they apply.
Der Radius wird eine Variable, und das M: The radius becomes a variable, and the mouse wheel adjusts it (code/loesungen/kap07_pinsel.dh):
MOUSE_WHEEL liefert, wie weit das Rad se: MOUSE_WHEEL returns how far the wheel has been turned since the last call, usually 0. CLAMP keeps the radius between 1 and 12. Instead of 9, the comparison now says radius ^ 2 — the 9 was the radius 3 squared, only without saying so.
Aus jedem y + 1 in den Regeln wird y + g: Every y + 1 in the rules becomes y + g, and the G key reverses g (code/loesungen/kap07_schwerkraft.dh):
Immer vom \"Boden\" her: bei g = -1 von: Always from the "floor": with g = -1 from top to bottom.
Was sich außer dem Fallen noch umdrehen: Apart from the falling, what also has to be turned around is the order of the step. It must always begin at the “floor”, otherwise a grain would fall all the way to the end in a single step — the mistake from “Why like this?”, only upwards. And the row it skips changes too: if everything falls upwards, nothing can fall any further in the top row, and the bottom row has to be computed as well.
Eine Möglichkeit (code/loesungen/kap07_f: One possibility (code/loesungen/kap07_feuer.dh): two new materials in the ENUM, a new rule for fire, one line in the SELECT CASE. Wood needs no rule; it lies there until fire reaches it:
Ist (x, y) im Feld und aus diesem Stoff?: Is (x, y) inside the grid and made of this material?
Feuer: steckt Holz in den vier Nachbarze: Fire: sets wood alight in the four neighbouring cells, rises
auf und erlischt mit der Zeit -- neben W: flickering and goes out over time -- next to water at once.

Zeile: die letzte rechnet schritt nie du: row: schritt never computes the last one (nothing falls there any more).
Die Zahlen 0.02 und 0.01 sind ausprobier: The numbers 0.02 and 0.01 were found by trying. With 0.2 instead of 0.02 the stack burns down in an instant; with 0.1 instead of 0.01 the fire goes out before it reaches the next wood. The flames get a random colour in every frame — that is why they flicker without needing any code of their own for it.
Nur noch eine Handvoll — acht, zehn Drei: Only a handful left — eight, ten triangles. The birds are all still there, but without separation, cohesion and alignment pull them onto one another until several fly exactly on top of each other, at the same speed, in the same direction. The rule that looks least like a flock is the very one that keeps it apart.
Kein Schwarm mehr, sondern ein Gewimmel: No flock any more, but a swirl like a cloud of midges. Birds gather into small clumps, but each one flies in its own direction, and the clumps fall apart again. Cohesion alone makes a heap; only alignment turns it into a flock that flies somewhere.
Mit SICHT 20 sieht ein Vogel kaum jemand: With SICHT 20 a bird hardly sees anyone. It takes a long time for small groups to find each other, and large flocks do not form. With 150 every bird sees almost half the sky: after a few seconds there are one or two big flocks, wide bands that sweep across the picture. The program has to compute the same amount in both cases, because umschauen always goes through all the birds — 150 times 150, a good twenty thousand distances in every frame.
Eine vierte Regel, gebaut wie der Zusamm: A fourth rule, built like cohesion, only with the mouse as the centre (code/loesungen/kap08_maus.dh):
Regel 4: zur Maus -- wie der Zusammenhal: Rule 4: towards the mouse -- like cohesion, but with the mouse
Der Aufruf steht nach dem IF nachbarn >: The call comes after the IF nachbarn > 0: even a bird flying on its own should head for the mouse. If you hold the button down for a long time, the flock circles around the mouse instead of landing on it — tempoHalten does not let it slow down, so it keeps overshooting.
Drei Felsen als drei Felder mit Mitte un: Three rocks as three arrays of centre and radius, and a rule that pushes the bird away from every rock it gets too close to (code/loesungen/kap08_hindernisse.dh):
Ab wie viel Abstand zum Rand ein Vogel a: How far from the edge a bird starts to swerve.
Regel 4: weg von jedem Felsen, dem der V: Rule 4: away from every rock the bird gets too close to -- the
closer to the edge, the stronger.
rand ist der Abstand vom Rand des Felsen: rand is the distance from the edge of the rock, not from its centre. st grows from 0, VORSICHT pixels before the edge, to 1 at the edge. So a bird swerves gently when it comes from far away, and sharply when it is almost there. Both numbers were found by trying: with KRAFT_FELS = 900 and VORSICHT = 30, in every fifth frame some bird was stuck in a rock, pushed by the flock behind it. Now it still happens, but rarely and only for a moment. Only bewegen could prevent it entirely, by not letting a bird in at all.
Eine Möglichkeit (code/loesungen/kap08_r: One possibility (code/loesungen/kap08_raubvogel.dh). The bird of prey is a bird too — it has a position and a velocity, it flies and comes back in at the edge. It just decides differently and looks different. That is exactly what EXTENDS says: Raubvogel gets everything from Vogel and replaces what it does differently. The birds get one more rule, fleeing:
Regel 4: weg vom Raubvogel, wenn er naeh: Rule 4: away from the bird of prey if it is closer than FLUCHT.
Der Raubvogel ist ein Vogel: Er erbt die: The bird of prey is a bird: it inherits the fields, Init and bewegen.
Nur entscheiden und zeichnen macht er an: It only does entscheiden and zeichnen differently.
Kein Schwarm fuer ihn: Er fliegt auf den: No flock for it: it flies towards the nearest bird.
Bewegen und Init schreibt der Raubvogel: The bird of prey does not write its own bewegen and Init;
dagegen ruft seine eigene Fassung. In i: instead calls its own version. In that version,
als NIL und wird der Vogel mit dem klei: starts as NIL and becomes the bird at the smallest distance. At 170, the bird of prey is a little slower than the fastest birds — otherwise the hunt would be over too quickly.
Mit einer Runde ist das Seil mal 300, ma: With one round the rope is sometimes 300, sometimes almost 390 long instead of 285, and it bounces like rubber: the links nudge their points into place, shift their neighbours in the process and get no second chance. With a hundred rounds it is exactly 285 long — and still looks the same as with twenty, because there it was 286 to 288, less than a tenth of a pixel per link. But a hundred rounds cost five times as much computing time. How many rounds you need is a trade-off, and the eye is the judge.
Mit 1.0 verliert das Seil keine Bewegung: With 1.0 the rope loses no motion: after ten seconds it still swings almost as far as at the start, and it never stops. With 0.95 it hangs still after three seconds, as if it were hanging in honey. 0.995 lies in between and swings on for a long time like a real rope. A number so close to 1 seems small, but it applies sixty times a second: 0.995 to the power of 60 is about 0.74 — a quarter less swing every second.
Die Fahrbahn hängt durch wie eine Hängem: The deck sags like a hammock. Measured, its middle sinks by 49 pixels without hangers and by 6 with them. Yet without hangers the deck has become only 10 pixels longer, 610 instead of 600 — each link gives a little, because twenty rounds never make it quite exact. A rope stretched between two points turns a small excess of length into a lot of sag. That is why suspension bridges carry their deck on a main cable: it sags anyway, and the deck can stay straight.
ziehen, fliegen, die Maus — alles bleibt: ziehen, fliegen, the mouse — everything stays. The only new thing is which points and which links there are (code/loesungen/kap09_vorhang.dh):
Ein Vorhang: SPALTEN mal ZEILEN Punkte i: A curtain: SPALTEN times ZEILEN points, 16 apart. The top
Reihe haengt an der Stange (fest); jeder: row hangs on the rod (fixed); every point is linked to its left
netz merkt sich, welche Nummer der Punkt: netz remembers which number the point in column sp and row ze was given; that way the neighbours can be found without working out in which order punkt created them. Six hundred points and a good thousand links, twenty times per step — that is the most this chapter computes, and it still runs smoothly.
Jedes Glied bekommt ein Feld, ob es noch: Every link gets an entry in an array that says whether it is still intact. If it gets more than 1.6 times as long as it should be, it snaps: it no longer pulls and is no longer drawn (code/loesungen/kap09_reissen.dh):
Ein Glied reisst, wenn es so viel mal la: A link snaps when it is this many times longer than it should be.
Wer die Mitte der Fahrbahn weit genug na: If you pull the middle of the deck down far enough, you tear it out: the piece falls into the water, and the two halves keep hanging from their hangers.
Gerissen wird nur in ziehen, und nur, we: Links snap only in ziehen, and only when the link is too long. It is usually the mouse that stretches it: a point the mouse holds does not give way, and the link next to it has to bear everything alone.
